``` # Learning objectives and overview This course introduces the principles of statistical testing through examples of commonly used tests. The examples draw on data from Gapminder and are illustrated with R and Python code. By the end of this session, you should be able to: - understand how statistical tests work; - test the distribution of a variable; - choose an appropriate test; - carry out tests in R or Python; - interpret the results of a test. # Data ## Gapminder data Gapminder provides a wide range of demographic, economic, social and environmental indicators for countries around the world. ### Exploring Gapminder data Explore how the relationship between gross domestic product (GDP) and life expectancy (`lex`) has changed since 1800. We will then work with these variables. ```{=html}

This video is available in the HTML version of the course.* ::: ### Drawing a random sample of `pop` values Here we randomly select 50 countries for which population data are available. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 5 set.seed(123) # Exclude rows where pop is missing (NA) data_filtre <- data_2025[!is.na(data_2025$pop), ] # Randomly select 50 rows without replacement echantillon_pop <- data_filtre[sample(nrow(data_filtre), 50), ] # Select the name, region and pop columns resultat <- echantillon_pop[, c("name", "region", "pop")] # Display the first 10 rows head(resultat, 10) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 10 × 3 name region pop 1 Ukraine europe 38980376 2 Bangladesh asia 175686899 3 Estonia europe 1344232 4 Oman asia 5494691 5 Denmark europe 6002507 6 Zambia africa 21913874 7 Yemen asia 41773878 8 Timor-Leste asia 1418517 9 Libya africa 7458555 10 Sri Lanka asia 23229470 ``` ::: ::: ### A histogram of the sample ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 6 # Draw a histogram of the selected variable hist(echantillon_pop$pop, breaks = 15, col = "steelblue", border = "white", main = "Random sample of 50 values", xlab = "Value", ylab = "Count") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Population distribution in a random sample of 50 countries.](index-en-r_files/figure-html/histogram-random-pop-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## How statistical tests work A statistical test usually starts with two hypotheses: - **H0**, the null hypothesis: no effect, no difference or no departure from a reference distribution; - **H1**, the alternative hypothesis: an effect, a difference or a departure from that distribution. The **p-value** is the probability of obtaining a result at least as extreme as the one observed, assuming that H0 is true. At the commonly used significance level of $\alpha = 0.05$: - if `p < 0.05`, we reject H0; - if `p >= 0.05`, we do not have sufficient evidence to reject H0. ::: {.content-visible when-format="html"} ```{=html}

``` [Open the video](https://mediaserver.unige.ch/play/319449). ::: ::: {.content-visible unless-format="html"} *From population to decision. This video is available in the HTML version of the course.* ::: We randomly generate 50 observations from a standard normal distribution, visualise their distribution and apply the **Shapiro–Wilk test**. For this test: - H0: the data are consistent with a normal distribution; - H1: the data are not consistent with a normal distribution. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 7 # Generate a random sample from a normal distribution set.seed(123) echantillon_normal <- rnorm( n = 50, mean = 0, sd = 1 ) # Draw a histogram hist(echantillon_normal, breaks = 12, col = "steelblue", border = "white", main = "Sample of 50 values from a normal distribution", xlab = "Value", ylab = "Count") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index-en-r_files/figure-html/normal-sample-1.png){width=672} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Test whether the sample follows a normal distribution shapiro.test(echantillon_normal) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Shapiro-Wilk normality test data: echantillon_normal W = 0.98928, p-value = 0.9279 ``` ::: ::: ### Example 2: a sample from a uniform distribution ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 8 # Generate a random sample from a uniform distribution set.seed(123) echantillon_uniforme <- runif( n = 50, min = 0, max = 1 ) hist(echantillon_uniforme, breaks = 12, col = "steelblue", border = "white", main = "Sample of 50 values from a uniform distribution", xlab = "Value", ylab = "Count") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index-en-r_files/figure-html/uniform-sample-1.png){width=672} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} shapiro.test(echantillon_uniforme) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Shapiro-Wilk normality test data: echantillon_uniforme W = 0.94599, p-value = 0.02341 ``` ::: ::: **Keep in mind:** with only 50 observations, a normality test may fail to detect a departure from normality. Interpret the test alongside the graphs. ### Example 3: testing the normality of `gdp` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 9 # Exclude missing GDP values gdp_complete <- data_2025$gdp_pcap[!is.na(data_2025$gdp_pcap)] # Visualise the data hist(gdp_complete, breaks = 30, col = "steelblue", border = "white", main = "Distribution of GDP per capita", xlab = "GDP per capita", ylab = "Number of countries") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index-en-r_files/figure-html/shapiro-gdp-1.png){width=672} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Test normality shapiro.test(gdp_complete) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Shapiro-Wilk normality test data: gdp_complete W = 0.82957, p-value = 8.206e-13 ``` ::: ::: ### Example 4: testing the normality of `lex` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 10 # Test the normality of LEX lex_complete <- data_2025$lex[!is.na(data_2025$lex)] hist(lex_complete, breaks = 30, col = "steelblue", border = "white", main = "Distribution of life expectancy across countries", xlab = "Life expectancy", ylab = "Number of countries") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index-en-r_files/figure-html/shapiro-lex-1.png){width=672} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} shapiro.test(lex_complete) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Shapiro-Wilk normality test data: lex_complete W = 0.95829, p-value = 5.903e-05 ``` ::: ::: ## Parametric or non-parametric? ::: {.content-visible when-format="html"} ```{=html}

``` [Open the video](https://mediaserver.unige.ch/play/319458). ::: ::: {.content-visible unless-format="html"} *Normality of the data. This video is available in the HTML version of the course.* ::: **Parametric tests** make assumptions about the distribution of the data or the residuals, often assuming normality. They generally have good power when these assumptions are reasonably satisfied. **Non-parametric tests** make fewer distributional assumptions and are often based on ranks. Their power relative to parametric tests depends on the data distribution and the assumptions of the tests being compared. | Question | Parametric | Non-parametric | |----------|------------|----------------| | Comparing 2 independent groups | Student’s t-test | Wilcoxon–Mann–Whitney | | Comparing more than 2 groups | ANOVA | Kruskal–Wallis | | Testing normality | Shapiro–Wilk | - | Do not base the choice solely on a normality test. Also examine the histograms, extreme values, sample sizes and assumptions of the test you are considering. ### Testing the normality of all quantitative variables ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 11 # Select the numeric variables in the data variables_quantitatives <- names(data_2025[,sapply(data_2025, is.numeric)]) # Create an empty data frame to store the results resultats_normalite = data.frame() # Loop over all quantitative variables for (variable in variables_quantitatives) { # Extract the values of this variable x = data_2025[[variable]] # Exclude missing or infinite values x = x[is.finite(x)] # Check whether the Shapiro–Wilk test can be applied if (length(x) >= 3 && length(x) <= 5000 && length(unique(x)) >= 3) { # Run the normality test test = shapiro.test(x) W = unname(test$statistic) p_value = test$p.value conclusion = ifelse(p_value < 0.05, "Normality rejected", "Normality not rejected") } else { W = NA p_value = NA conclusion = "Test not applicable" } # Create a row of results ligne = data.frame( variable = variable, n = length(x), W = W, p_value = p_value, conclusion = conclusion ) # Add the row to the results table resultats_normalite = rbind(resultats_normalite, ligne) } # Display the completed table print(resultats_normalite) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` variable n W p_value conclusion 1 pop 170 0.2522057 8.456179e-26 Normality rejected 2 lex 170 0.9582896 5.902530e-05 Normality rejected 3 gdp_pcap 170 0.8295702 8.206441e-13 Normality rejected 4 area_km2 170 0.3837491 8.021477e-24 Normality rejected 5 ind_water 164 0.7634311 5.584184e-15 Normality rejected 6 agr_water 165 0.9026782 5.455825e-09 Normality rejected 7 wat_with 165 0.2759994 3.991601e-25 Normality rejected 8 hydropower 118 0.3338533 8.397743e-21 Normality rejected 9 prec 168 0.9403098 1.726468e-06 Normality rejected 10 co2 170 0.7884745 2.095536e-14 Normality rejected 11 primary_forest_area 169 0.2408209 6.872195e-26 Normality rejected 12 en_mam 170 0.6369434 7.639315e-19 Normality rejected 13 en_fsh 170 0.8071810 1.039313e-13 Normality rejected 14 en_brd 170 0.6788610 8.874299e-18 Normality rejected 15 en_thrd 170 0.4954091 7.227605e-22 Normality rejected 16 PA_land 170 0.9673096 4.936411e-04 Normality rejected 17 PA_marine 133 0.7261484 1.918315e-14 Normality rejected 18 denspop 170 0.6614419 3.116633e-18 Normality rejected ``` ::: ::: ### Histograms of all quantitative variables ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 12 # Identify the numeric variables variables_quantitatives = names(data_2025)[sapply(data_2025, is.numeric)] # Arrange the plots in rows and columns par(mfrow = c(3, 3)) # Draw a histogram for each variable for (variable in variables_quantitatives) { hist(data_2025[[variable]], main = variable, xlab = "Value", ylab = "Count", col = "steelblue", border = "white", breaks = 12) } ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index-en-r_files/figure-html/histograms-all-numeric-1.png){width=1056} ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index-en-r_files/figure-html/histograms-all-numeric-2.png){width=1056} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Restore the usual plotting layout par(mfrow = c(1, 1)) ``` ::: ## Comparing means ::: {.content-visible when-format="html"} ```{=html}

``` [Open the video](https://mediaserver.unige.ch/play/319450). ::: ::: {.content-visible unless-format="html"} *Comparing means and understanding ANOVA. This video is available in the HTML version of the course.* ::: Here we compare **Europe** and **Africa**. ### Life expectancy in European and African countries ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 13 # Extract data for the two regions europe_afrique <- data_2025[data_2025$region %in% c("europe", "africa"), ] # Draw histograms for the two regions ggplot( europe_afrique, aes(x = lex) ) + geom_histogram(bins = 20, na.rm = TRUE, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white", linewidth = 0.4) + facet_wrap( ~ region, scales = "free_y" ) + labs( title = "Life expectancy in European and African countries", x = "Life expectancy", y = "Number of countries" ) + theme_minimal() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index-en-r_files/figure-html/hist-lex-europe-africa-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: ### Student’s t-test We compare the means of the two groups. The hypotheses are: - H0: mean life expectancy is the same in Europe and Africa; - H1: mean life expectancy differs between the two regions. The classical Student’s t-test assumes independent observations, approximate normality within each group and equal variances. Here, `var.equal = TRUE` explicitly requests the classical version of the test. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 14 test_student <- t.test( lex ~ region, data = europe_afrique, var.equal = TRUE ) test_student ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Two Sample t-test data: lex by region t = -14.949, df = 93, p-value < 2.2e-16 alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group africa and group europe is not equal to 0 95 percent confidence interval: -15.36433 -11.76104 sample estimates: mean in group africa mean in group europe 66.17173 79.73442 ``` ::: ::: ### The Wilcoxon–Mann–Whitney test This non-parametric test compares the ranks of observations in the two groups. It does not require normality. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 15 test_wilcoxon <- wilcox.test( lex ~ region, data = europe_afrique, exact = FALSE ) test_wilcoxon ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction data: lex by region W = 39, p-value = 7.384e-16 alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0 ``` ::: ::: > The Wilcoxon–Mann–Whitney test is often described as a comparison of distributions. More specifically, it tests for a shift in ranks. Interpreting it as a comparison of medians requires, in particular, distributions with similar shapes. ## Comparing more than 2 means ### Life expectancy in the four regions ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 16 # Select data for the four regions four_regions <- data_2025[data_2025$region %in% c("europe", "africa", "asia","americas"), ] # Draw histograms by region ggplot(four_regions, aes(x = lex, fill = region)) + geom_histogram( bins = 20, colour = "white", alpha = 0.85 ) + facet_wrap( ~ region, scales = "free_y" ) + scale_x_log10( labels = scales::label_number(big.mark = " ") ) + labs( title = "Distribution of life expectancy", subtitle = "Comparing the four continents", x = "LEX", y = "Number of countries" ) + guides(fill = "none") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index-en-r_files/figure-html/hist-lex-four-regions-1.png){width=960} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Draw a boxplot by region ggplot( four_regions, aes( x = region, y = lex, fill = region ) ) + geom_boxplot( width = 0.65, alpha = 0.7, outlier.shape = NA ) + geom_jitter( width = 0.15, alpha = 0.5, size = 1.8 ) + labs( title = "Life expectancy by region", subtitle = "Comparing the four continents", x = NULL, y = "Years" ) + guides(fill = "none") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index-en-r_files/figure-html/hist-lex-four-regions-2.png){width=960} ::: ::: ### ANOVA tests whether all the means can be considered equal - H0: the four regions have the same mean life expectancy; - H1: at least one mean differs. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 17 modele_anova <- aov( lex ~ region, data = four_regions ) summary(modele_anova) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F) region 3 4738 1579 75.35 <2e-16 *** Residuals 166 3480 21 --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ::: A significant ANOVA result tells us that at least one mean differs, but not which one. Tukey’s post-hoc test allows us to explore pairwise differences: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 18 TukeyHSD(modele_anova) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Tukey multiple comparisons of means 95% family-wise confidence level Fit: aov(formula = lex ~ region, data = four_regions) $region diff lwr upr p adj americas-africa 9.6482692 6.863092 12.433446 0.0000000 asia-africa 8.9829501 6.591532 11.374368 0.0000000 europe-africa 13.5626878 11.113543 16.011832 0.0000000 asia-americas -0.6653191 -3.501874 2.171236 0.9291944 europe-americas 3.9144186 1.029029 6.799808 0.0030917 europe-asia 4.5797378 2.072321 7.087155 0.0000270 ``` ::: ::: ### Checking the ANOVA residuals The normality assumption mainly concerns the **model residuals**, rather than necessarily the raw variable itself. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 19 # Extract the ANOVA residuals residus_anova <- residuals(modele_anova) # Check the normality of the residuals shapiro.test(residus_anova) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Shapiro-Wilk normality test data: residus_anova W = 0.99144, p-value = 0.407 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Draw a histogram of the residuals hist(residus_anova, breaks = 20, probability = TRUE, col = "steelblue", border = "white", main = "Distribution of ANOVA residuals", xlab = "Residuals", ylab = "Density") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index-en-r_files/figure-html/anova-diagnostics-1.png){width=768} ::: ::: ### The Kruskal–Wallis test The Kruskal–Wallis test is a non-parametric alternative to one-way ANOVA. - H0: the groups have comparable rank distributions; - H1: at least one group differs. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 20 # Compare the regions using a non-parametric test test_kruskal <- kruskal.test( lex ~ region, data = four_regions ) test_kruskal ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test data: lex by region Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared = 93.585, df = 3, p-value < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ::: ## Independence between two categorical variables: the χ² test The previous tests compared a quantitative variable across groups. The **chi-square test of independence** looks for an association between **two categorical variables**, using a table of counts. ### The question and the variables Is the proportion of countries with a life expectancy of at least 75 years the same in all four regions? We use the same dataset: - `region`: the region of the world; - `classe_lex`: life expectancy below 75 years, or at least 75 years. The threshold of 75 years is chosen for this exercise before looking at the result. Turning a quantitative variable into categories loses information. Here, we do so to illustrate the chi-square test. ### Preparing the data Each country must appear only once and belong to a single category for each variable. Missing values are excluded. ::: {.content-visible when-format="html"} ```{=html}

``` [Open the video](https://mediaserver.unige.ch/play/319448). ::: ::: {.content-visible unless-format="html"} *The chi-square test of independence. This video is available in the HTML version of the course.* ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 21 # Keep only valid life-expectancy values donnees_chi2 <- subset(four_regions, is.finite(lex)) # Treat region as a categorical variable donnees_chi2$region <- factor(donnees_chi2$region) # Create two life-expectancy categories donnees_chi2$classe_lex <- ifelse(donnees_chi2$lex < 75, "Under 75 years", "75 years or older") # Store the categories in their intended order donnees_chi2$classe_lex <- factor( donnees_chi2$classe_lex, levels = c("Under 75 years", "75 years or older") ) # Display the first 10 observations head(donnees_chi2[, c("name", "region", "lex", "classe_lex")], 10) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 10 × 4 name region lex classe_lex 1 Afghanistan asia 69.3 Under 75 years 2 Angola africa 64.9 Under 75 years 3 Albania europe 80.1 75 years or older 4 UAE asia 80.6 75 years or older 5 Argentina americas 78 75 years or older 6 Armenia europe 80.1 75 years or older 7 Australia asia 84.3 75 years or older 8 Austria europe 82.4 75 years or older 9 Azerbaijan europe 73.1 Under 75 years 10 Burundi africa 62.2 Under 75 years ``` ::: ::: ### Building the contingency table A **contingency table** cross-tabulates the categories of the two variables. Each cell contains a count of countries, not a percentage. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 22 # Create the contingency table tableau_chi2 <- xtabs( ~ region + classe_lex, data = donnees_chi2 ) # Observed counts and totals addmargins(tableau_chi2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` classe_lex region Under 75 years 75 years or older Sum africa 47 5 52 americas 11 17 28 asia 24 23 47 europe 3 40 43 Sum 85 85 170 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Percentages within each region round(100 * prop.table(tableau_chi2, margin = 1), 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` classe_lex region Under 75 years 75 years or older africa 90.4 9.6 americas 39.3 60.7 asia 51.1 48.9 europe 7.0 93.0 ``` ::: ::: ### Visualising the proportions ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 23 # Plot the life-expectancy categories in each region ggplot(donnees_chi2, aes(x = region, fill = classe_lex)) + geom_bar(position = "fill", colour = "white") + scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) + scale_fill_manual(values = c("#D98C45", "#4682B4")) + labs( title = "Life expectancy and world region", subtitle = "Each region represents 100% of its countries", x = "Region", y = "Proportion of countries", fill = "Life expectancy" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Distribution of life-expectancy categories within each region.](index-en-r_files/figure-html/chi2-proportions-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: ### Formulating the hypotheses - **H0:** region and life-expectancy category are independent. The proportions in the two categories are the same across regions in the reference population. - **H1:** the two variables are associated. At least one region has a different distribution across the categories. Under H0, the expected count in each cell is: $$ E_{ij} = \frac{\text{total for row } i \times \text{total for column } j} {\text{overall count}} $$ The test statistic measures the discrepancy between the observed and expected counts: $$ \chi^2 = \sum_{i,j} \frac{(O_{ij} - E_{ij})^2}{E_{ij}} $$ Larger discrepancies produce a larger statistic. For a table with four regions and two categories, the degrees of freedom are $(4-1)(2-1)=3$. ### Checking the expected counts The chi-square approximation requires sufficiently large expected counts. A common rule of thumb is: - no expected count below 1; - at least 80% of the expected counts equal to or greater than 5. These conditions concern the **expected counts**, not the observed counts. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 24 # Calculate the expected counts under H0 effectifs_attendus <- outer( rowSums(tableau_chi2), colSums(tableau_chi2) ) / sum(tableau_chi2) dimnames(effectifs_attendus) <- dimnames(tableau_chi2) round(effectifs_attendus, 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` classe_lex region Under 75 years 75 years or older africa 26.0 26.0 americas 14.0 14.0 asia 23.5 23.5 europe 21.5 21.5 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} conditions_chi2 <- all(effectifs_attendus >= 1) && mean(effectifs_attendus >= 5) >= 0.80 conditions_chi2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ::: ### Running the test If the expected counts are large enough, we use the usual approximation. Otherwise, we calculate a p-value using Monte Carlo simulation. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 25 # Run the chi-square test set.seed(123) if (conditions_chi2) { test_chi2 <- chisq.test(tableau_chi2, correct = FALSE) } else { test_chi2 <- chisq.test( tableau_chi2, simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 99999 ) } test_chi2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Pearson's Chi-squared test data: tableau_chi2 X-squared = 67.067, df = 3, p-value = 1.812e-14 ``` ::: ::: For a 2 × 2 table with small expected counts, Fisher’s exact test is another common option: `fisher.test(tableau)`. ### Interpreting the result ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 26 cat( "Method:", test_chi2$method, "\nChi-square statistic:", round(unname(test_chi2$statistic), 2), "\np-value:", format.pval(test_chi2$p.value, digits = 3), "\n\n" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Method: Pearson's Chi-squared test Chi-square statistic: 67.07 p-value: 1.81e-14 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} if (test_chi2$p.value < 0.05) { cat( "At the 5% significance level, we reject H0:", "the data indicate an association between region", "and life-expectancy category." ) } else { cat( "At the 5% significance level, we do not reject H0:", "the data do not provide sufficient evidence of an association.", "This does not establish independence." ) } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` At the 5% significance level, we reject H0: the data indicate an association between region and life-expectancy category. ``` ::: ::: A significant result indicates an **association**. It does not establish that region causes the differences in life expectancy. ### Measuring the strength of association: Cramér’s V The p-value does not measure the strength of the association. **Cramér’s V** complements the test and ranges from 0 to 1. A value close to 0 indicates a weak association. Its importance should be interpreted in the context of the study. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 27 n_chi2 <- sum(tableau_chi2) v_cramer <- sqrt( unname(test_chi2$statistic) / (n_chi2 * min(nrow(tableau_chi2) - 1, ncol(tableau_chi2) - 1)) ) data.frame( "number_of_countries" = n_chi2, "V_Cramer" = v_cramer ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` number_of_countries V_Cramer 1 170 0.628103 ``` ::: ::: ### Limitations of this example The test assumes independent observations. However, countries may share geographical, historical or economic characteristics. Moreover, these data are a collection of countries with available information, rather than a random sample. Statistical inference therefore remains conditional on these assumptions. The conclusions apply only to the countries retained after filtering and to the categories defined by the 75-year threshold. # Interpreting tests We can follow four steps when interpreting a statistical test: 1. **State H0 and H1** before looking at the result. 2. **Check the test assumptions** and examine the data graphically. 3. **Read the p-value** and compare it with the significance level $\alpha$, often set to 0.05. 4. **Interpret the effect in context**, going beyond “significant” or “not significant”. Statistical significance alone does not tell us how important a difference is in practice. It is also useful to examine means or medians, variability, effect sizes and confidence intervals. # Summary: which test should we choose? The choice depends first on the types of variables, the question being asked and whether the observations are independent or paired. The table below concerns comparisons of independent groups. | Aim | Variables | Groups | Main assumptions and considerations | Test | |--------------------|--------------------|---------------|-------------------------|--------------------| | Test normality | One quantitative variable or a set of residuals | - | 3 to 5,000 values; supplement with a histogram and a Q–Q plot | Shapiro–Wilk | | Compare two means | One quantitative and one categorical variable | 2 | Independent observations; approximate normality within groups or sufficiently large samples; sensitivity to extreme values | Welch’s t-test; Student’s t-test if equal variances are justified | | Compare two distributions using ranks | One quantitative or ordinal variable and one categorical variable | 2 | Independent observations; similar distribution shapes to interpret a difference in location | Wilcoxon–Mann–Whitney | | Compare several means | One quantitative and one categorical variable | More than 2 | Independent observations; approximately normal residuals; comparable variances | Classical ANOVA; Welch’s ANOVA if variances differ | | Compare several distributions using ranks | One quantitative or ordinal variable and one categorical variable | More than 2 | Independent observations; similar distribution shapes to interpret a difference in location | Kruskal–Wallis | | Test an association between categories | Two categorical variables | At least 2 categories per variable | Independent country observations; sufficiently large expected counts | Chi-square test of independence | | Test an association with small counts | Two categorical variables | At least 2 categories per variable | Examine the expected counts and the dimensions of the table | Fisher’s exact test, particularly for 2 × 2 tables, or a chi-square test with a simulated p-value | **Key points:** - Do not choose a test solely on the basis of Shapiro–Wilk. - When comparing means, examine distributions within groups and model residuals, rather than just the overall distribution. - The chi-square test uses counts, not percentages directly. - A significant association does not demonstrate causality. - Always complement the p-value with graphs and a measure of the size of the effect. # Questions about this session {#questions-session-04} If a concept is still unclear, you would like to explore an example further, or you have any other question, feel free to ask it in the SpeakUp space below (anonymously or not).
